description:
We are Team S.T.A.R.S. We are working on the Flame in Freefall challenge to build a smart, automated fire safety and suppression system for space habitats.

Our team covers process engineering, control engineering, electronics, data science, UI design, and business strategy. Our goal is to build a practical, high-tech safety solution for future space habitats.!
summary:
We developed "Flame in Freefall", an interactive platform that makes NASA's microgravity combustion research easier to explore, understand, and use. The project brings together data from NASA combustion investigations in one place, allowing users to search and compare experiments, explore experimental conditions, investigate fire-suppression behavior, and ask questions about the research through an AI-assisted interface with links to supporting sources.

The idea addresses the challenge of turning decades of NASA research into information that is more accessible and useful for understanding fire behavior in space. By connecting experimental data with interactive exploration tools, we aim to help users identify relevant findings, compare results, and better understand the challenges of fire safety in microgravity.

This matters because as human missions extend to the Moon and Mars, understanding how fire behaves in space is essential for designing safer spacecraft and habitats. Our platform is a step toward making that research more accessible to the people working on those challenges.
details:
Project Details — Flame in Freefall

Flame in Freefall is an interactive research and decision-support platform designed to make NASA's microgravity combustion research easier to explore, compare, and interpret for spacecraft fire safety. Fire behaves differently in microgravity because buoyancy-driven convection is greatly reduced, changing flame shape, oxygen transport, and smoke behaviour. This creates important challenges for future space habitats, especially on the Moon and Mars.

Our platform brings together data from 24 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion investigations. We collected and organized 22 experimental data tables into a unified dataset containing 2,009 test records, while preserving links to their original NASA sources. The platform allows users to search and compare investigations, filter experimental conditions, visualize relationships between variables, and explore research according to three fire-safety themes: prevention, detection, and suppression.

One of the main features is the Suppression Lab, based on NASA's Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX). It uses experimental methanol and heptane droplet data to explore how conditions such as oxygen concentration, pressure, droplet size, and suppressant concentration affect flame behaviour. We developed machine-learning models to estimate burning rate and extinction behaviour, with uncertainty ranges and validation results to help users understand how reliable the predictions are.

Another feature is Ask NASA Records, an AI-assisted research interface. Users can ask questions in natural language and receive answers grounded in retrieved NASA documents and experimental records. The system retrieves relevant passages and displays their sources, helping users verify the information instead of relying on unsupported AI-generated answers.

The project also highlights an important result from the FLEX analysis: under the modelled conditions, approximately 40% CO₂ was associated with near-immediate flame extinction, with a best estimate around 45%. However, this is a research finding within the tested droplet-experiment conditions, not a recommendation for spacecraft fire suppression. CO₂ also reduces oxygen concentration, and droplet experiments cannot directly represent fires involving spacecraft cabin materials. We therefore display these limitations and the model's uncertainty alongside the results.

Benefits and intended impact: The platform makes decades of NASA research more accessible and useful to students, researchers, aerospace engineers, and space-safety specialists. It can help users identify relevant experiments, compare evidence, investigate suppression conditions, and recognize gaps in existing research. Our long-term goal is to support better-informed fire-safety research and the development of safer human space habitats.

Tools and technologies: We used Python for data processing, scientific analysis, machine-learning models, and the Streamlit application; Next.js for the web dashboard; scikit-learn for machine learning and TF-IDF-based document retrieval; Plotly for interactive data visualization; and the Google Gemini API for AI-assisted, source-grounded explanations. We also used NASA's public PSI data and API, GitHub for version control and source-code management, Streamlit Community Cloud and Vercel for deployment, and Claude Code as a development assistant under our team's direction.

Creativity and design considerations: The creative aspect of our project is not simply displaying NASA data, but connecting scientific records, data analysis, machine learning, and AI-assisted research in one accessible platform. We designed the system around traceability, scientific reliability, transparency, and usability. We considered differences in experimental units, missing or ambiguous values, the limits of available gravity conditions, model uncertainty, and the risk of AI producing unsupported conclusions. Rather than hiding these limitations, we make them visible so that users can distinguish experimental evidence from model estimates and interpretations.
